utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We're grateful to the witness for being here, and if the general would take the declaration part, which he has to cover for him, now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's General Vegh. Your curriculum vitae is before the Court in a document that I will produce in a second, with their leave. It reveals that you've been a soldier effectively all of your working life with relevant training, inter alia, in Moscow at the Military Academy of Tank Units and also in the Army War College in the United States of America, a person who has, I think, obtained a Ph.D. on a military subject which you list; and, General, you achieved the rank of Deputy Chief of the General Staff of the Hungarian defence forces in 1995 and rose to the rank of commander of the Hungarian defence forces and Chief of the General Staff in 1996, a position you held until 1999, thereafter being appointed ambassador of Hungary to Turkey between the years 2000 and 2002, and the conclusion of that part of your career is that you then suffered a very serious car accident from which you are suffering -- from which you are now undergoing and enjoying rehabilitation, and that explains why you were seated when you took the solemn declaration; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could we just ask -- could we just ask for one minute to be allowed. Just a moment, please. Thank you. If you'd just wait one moment while we consider this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's Hungarian interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. I understand the position fully. Yes, let's go on. If the general could continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the accused had a concern. It may be he's overlooked that he has to plug his earpiece into a different socket.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm receiving the Serbian interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think that is the way it is to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I'm afraid I had understood in advance that there was going to be simultaneous translation or interpretation. I'm not sure why that isn't the case, and it's no doubt my oversight, for which I apologise not checking the administration in advance, but we will do the best we can. I will tailor my questions and the amount of evidence I ask of the witness to the restricted facilities that come without simultaneous interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that the Hungarian conference interpreters are in the booth to translate the general from Hungarian to English but not in Budapest on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's what I understood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us continue, but we need to go back to the General's curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to trouble you, but we are now again not getting the right picture. Yes. We now have it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, the -- first of all, can I check with the staff in -- can I just check one administrative matter. General, are you, in fact, hearing me in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position is that in fact I had a conversation with the general shortly before we started this morning. His English is impeccable, it's the mechanism for his hearing which is impaired. It may be, if I could ask Ms. Anoya -- it may be that we could speed the process up if the general is able to understand my questions in English, to reply in Hungarian and to have the benefit of the interpreter in the booth here. Can I ask Ms. Anoya to investigate that. I think she can hear what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. General, can you hear the English when Mr. Nice is speaking to you? Can you hear it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can -- I can hear it, but in a very limited way, and this is why I absolutely require interpreting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case I'll --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, your report dated the 26th of January of this year is in two parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can the interpreter translate that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, can you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your report of the 26th of January is in two parts.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes, it does comprise two parts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to deal effectively only with the conclusions of each part in order to maximise the time available for the accused to ask you questions. The rest the report, which has, I think, been publicly filed, speaking for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I could listen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. One at a time. We'll deal with it in a moment. If there is some difficulty, would you go and speak to the officer. Would you go and ask him? Would you just wait for a moment and speak to him. Let's do one thing at a time. Yes. Let's continue for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I trust that the Chamber now has the paragraph numbered versions of the report which were filed for ease of reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Would you give us those, please, what they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The paragraph number of the report to which I'm turning, which is the conclusions, is at paragraph 125 and onwards, page 24 in the English version of the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, General Vegh, again, you were asked to prepare a report from the position of a senior officer with experience of Warsaw Pact forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You reviewed a quantity of documentation, and I think you also reviewed the experts' reports produced by the Office of the Prosecutor under the names of Reynaud Theunens and also including the name of Allen Borrelli; correct?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. All those documents and my own experience were the basis for my answers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 126 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you have to wait. The Serbian interpreters begin their interpretation after having the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At paragraph 126, you express your opinion that at the collapse of the supreme state leadership, the armed forces became a tool for achieving political objectives. In a couple of sentences only, please expand on paragraph 126.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Your Honour, the defence forces, they carried out their tasks. The armed leader -- the supreme state leadership carried out their tasks. At the same force, the Territorial Defence forces, which were also part of the defence forces, were not subordinated during peacetimes to the SFRY. They were subordinated to the republic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. When the crisis broke out, the defence for the Territorial Defence forces dissolved and were reorganised, and that was a problem for the leadership.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 127, you express the view that commanders of local units would not have been able to distribute weapons to local inhabitants without superior orders. Does that remain your clear view from the material you've reviewed?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, I'm still of the same opinion. The commanders of the local military units cannot have the right to give arms to any group which are not part of the military units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 129. At what stage should volunteers and paramilitary forces have been regulated so as to fall under the control of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Your Honours, of course, it -- during -- in the armed forces --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the general please repeat this. Could you ask the general to repeat this, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Generally speaking, the armed forces and the military forces who defend the territory belong to the armed forces, and the -- and because the reorganisation of the armed forces at that time, the local defence force -- local defence forces were formed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, one moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And also other groups. Other groups were forming combat units. These groups can only get tasks when they are subordinated to the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One moment. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am only getting excerpts in the Serbian language, just a word here and there, and they have been interrupted with the words spoken by General Vegh. I really can't understand anything he's saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do the best you can. You must do the best you can and answer any questions as we can and do the best that we can in the present circumstances. Yes, let's go on. We have it in English, and you also have the report, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, so far as your conclusions in relation to Croatia are concerned, paragraph 130, you express views on the inadequacy of the maintenance of discipline, finding from the materials that maintenance of discipline was not fully implemented. The question to which I would like an answer is whether in your judgement the army had the mechanism of a modern army sufficient to maintain discipline had it chosen to do so.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to say first of all that I don't have any direct experiences. The documents which I had, the laws, the regulations, the publications which I had at my disposal were the basis for my conclusions regarding as to how the army could have worked, and I concluded that the army of the Yugoslav Republic at that time was organised and was led according to the doctrines and the regulations in force at that time, and there was a possibility to keep to the rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I turn to --

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: At this same time, one can also see that the -- the circumstances were such that the -- that there were very negative trends, and those were mostly -- had mostly undesirable effects as far as the implication of the doctrines was concerned, the practical implication. For example, there could have been two standards for the -- for judging certain circumstances or certain cases, or as far as judging the tolerance and the sanctions is concerned. There were several cases where theory and practice were not congruent or at least doubtful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will allow the objection -- let him finish. What is it you want to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I'm listening to and hearing, I can conclude, and I'm sure that Mr. Tapuskovic will bear me out, that the witness is speaking, after that we hear the English interpretation, and then after the English interpretation we have the Serbian interpretation. However, it overlaps. The Serbian interpretation is still ongoing when the general starts speaking again. So we should make a pause, wait for the Serbian interpretation to finish, otherwise there is overlapping between the Serbian and what the general is saying, and I can't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If that is the case, it should be put right. We will do that, if it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will ask Ms. Dicklich to tell me when the Serbian version is concluded and I'll start my next question. Thank you. There have been a few very detailed corrections, mostly to footnotes, that the general has told me about. Rather than take time now, I can deal with those at the conclusion of his evidence. I turn to the conclusions in the Bosnia report. The majority of the report speaking for itself, I take the Court and the general to paragraph 257, English page 48.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Has everybody -- has everybody got a picture, has got the time? They were late.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think everybody has got them now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At paragraph 257, and between there and paragraph 271, you deal with Operation Drina 93. In a couple of sentences, please, the significance of this document for the interrelationship of the three armies to which you refer; the SVK, the VJ, and the VRS.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Operation Drina 93 was a strategic plan. A strategic plan is usually worked out by the leadership. The leadership carry out their tasks according to their political aims and goals. The Drina plan had two components; first of all, it assumes that the war, the crisis, could expand to the whole region. The strategic plan determines the -- the aims -- aims as far as counteracting the aggression is concerned. The Krajina army and the Bosnian army --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the general please repeat. Could the general please repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Krajina Serbian army and the Bosnian Serbian army had detailed tasks for -- for spring of 1994. This plan belongs to the logistic and air defence plans of Yugoslavia. The second phase of this plan concerns the cooperation of the Serbian states in case of aggression. In this phase, the plan is counting on the active cooperation of the Yugoslav army and also on the logistic support. This plan was worked out by the leadership of the Bosnian Serb army and the Chief of Staff has signed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: I think that since three different armies are involved here, or at least their cooperation is involved here, the Chiefs of Staff certainly were involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the --

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the general please repeat this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This -- this plan was probably drawn up on the basis of a step-by-step plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, General, that's enough. And the translation has finished. The time taken, General, requires us to be careful in our use of it, and if we move beyond your analysis of the combat readiness for the VRS in 1992 covered at 272 to 279, which is self-explanatory, we come to paragraph 280. Does -- at paragraph 280, you deal with the Gvozd Operation in February 1995. For economic use of time, should the reader of the report be focusing on this operation, as you describe it, for the similar purpose, namely the degree of interrelationship between the armies that the plan reveals?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. What is it? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite simply, I don't think there should be any overlapping in the interpretation. While the Serbian interpreter is translating, the Hungarian interpreter is doing the same and then we get Serbian and Hungarian at the same time so I can't understand what is being said in Serbian. They have to wait for each other to finish. If we have three languages, Serbian, English and Hungarian, each interpreter has to wait or the other to finish, otherwise, there is general overlapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Indeed. We will ensure that matters are dealt with as far as possible today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my last question, in light of the time difficulties and constraints: You were asked to express other conclusions, which you have done, but at the very end of your report, 299, you were asked to focus on the possible issue which may arise from language used by people at certain points in chains of command, namely the phrase "one army" to describe the connection between the VRS and the VJ. Again, just in a couple of sentences, General, if you can, your view from all the material on the appropriateness or not of the phrase "one army."

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Honourable Tribunal, in several records and several reports, we see the expression "one army, own forces." This expression is used quite often in every case where there is military cooperation. Generally speaking, this is used in order to distinguish "own forces." And also, it is a matter of recognising each other, mutual recognition. There are various signs and symbols that serve the purpose of distinguishing in this respect, and when you talk about one army or two separate armies, and this I'm referring to as a theory, we can imagine different approaches to this question. The most basic approach would be a distinction made on an emotional basis, and this would mean that forces fighting on the same side carry out their tasks in very close cooperation. They have common aims, common goals, and at the same time, it is also possible that the commanders and the soldiers of the military actually know each other. And there can also be a similarity as regards organisation. If we try to explain this using political arguments, and I'm still talking about one army or two armies, then on the basis of the documents that had been made available to me, it is very clear that the political and legal grounds did in fact exist for the separation of the two armies. Both the military and the political leadership control and command had separate systems, and the structure that came into being as a result of that did function and guaranteed independent functioning. If we look at it from the military point of view, then we can state that as a result of joint activities, there could be a very close cooperation between the two armies, the two armed forces. And at the same time, there could be a very strong logistical support. Therefore, two armed forces working in close cooperation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: And if we look at the question from the point of view of the military logistical support, then we can conclude that previously the JNA had a joint central logistical support system. But after -- after the withdrawal, there was -- there were two separate systems. But at the same time, the system of subordination prevailed. And therefore, from the logistical point of view, we can talk about one army providing support to another army. Therefore, there were two armed forces working jointly, cooperating very closely --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: -- with each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I sit down, I thought I heard on line 23 of the previous page "juristical point of view," but it reads "logistical point of view." I don't know if the interpreters can assist me with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be simpler to deal with the matter later rather than spend time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's only one correction that the witness told me about that's in the body of the report. That's the only one I'll deal with now. He doesn't need to comment on it. It's at page 13, paragraph 73. Last sentence reads, "He coordinates the combined operations of service branches." The witness wishes the word "combined" to be replaced by "joined." It's the same topic that we're dealing with in another part of the report. I can deal with footnote corrections, if material, later. Thank you, General Vegh, you will be asked further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is your number for this, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 644. And may the curriculum vitae be separately exhibited, or tab 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we have that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I would -- thank you, General, you will be asked further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the interpreters interpose for a second? We have a suggestion. If the Hungarian consecutive interpreter on the spot could be asked to cut her microphone when she is speaking to the general, then we would not hear her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let us see if that improves, see how we get on. Yes, you've got two hours to ask some questions, if you wish, Mr. Milosevic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we can just have one minute to deal with the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We can go on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I keep hearing some noise. I can't -- do you hear that too?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Don't be concerned about that. Just try and concentrate on what you can and hear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well, Mr. May. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Vegh, in the beginning of your report, you stated, and I'm quoting: "I was requested to describe the functions of the military command and control system and its theoretical and practical aspects and to draw conclusions that have a significant bearing on the case." My question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness finish the question and then we'll continue. Yes. Has the matter not been repeated? Is that the difficulty, the report?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, Your Honour, we're just hearing silence while the Hungarian interpreter is interpreting to the general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is what I was asked to do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But actually, we didn't hear the accused's question as he could note from the transcript. What was your question, Mr. Milosevic? Was your question whether it was right or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't even ask the question, I just quoted from the general's report that he was requested to derive conclusions which bear on the case. That's the quotation, and my question is: When you say "in the army," I suppose you mean in armies in general, not a specific individual army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes. This is the case. Generally speaking, I was writing about the way armed forces function, but there are certain specific cases in which in the question you asked me concrete points, and in that case I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. refer to those concrete points in my answers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. I understand, General Vegh. Now my question is: In your opinion, the systems of command and control in various armies in the world, in civilised countries, I mean, are they very different across the board or do they tend to be similar?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Honourable Jury, command and control tends to be similar in different armed forces because every time we talk about organisations of hierarchical set-up, there is one person in charge of subordination, a command control and norms of discipline and activities following the doctrines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say in this written report that part of your task was to derive, and I quote: "Conclusions which have a significant bearing on the case." Which case do you mean?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Basically, I was asked questions based on the Croatian crisis pertaining to the different characteristics of the Yugoslav People's Army at that time, how I consider the leadership, command and control of this army, how the doctrines could function in reality, in practice, what was the system of discipline and the morale of the troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, you say: "The conclusions I drew about the operations in Croatia with particular attention to the activities of the armed forces in Yugoslavia are based on the materials, orders, and regulations placed at my disposal as well as on my own research." My question is, General, when you say "operations," do you imply all the combat activities in 1991?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. And I only have direct [as interpreted] experiences. Those documents which were put at my disposal and my own experience were the basis for my findings, and I only answered on the basis of the questions asked how the armed forces could have functioned or should have functioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, General. Thank you. Now, in paragraph 3, you state that by that so-called Prosecution you were asked to refer exclusively to those documents which their team placed at your disposal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I only worked on the basis of the documents I received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, General. However, would you please explain one thing to me. In point 3, you say that they - that is to say the people from the so-called Prosecution - asked you, "For the purposes of my report --" and I am quoting you, and to -- on the assumption -- "any analysis or conclusions I made were done so on the presumption that any accusations, facts and documents given to me are factually correct." And you use the word "accusations." "... presumption that any accusations, facts and documents given to me are factually correct." I should like to underline that in your own paragraph 3. And so you say: "Finally, I have been invited to assume the facts of the case are correct for the purposes of my report, and to refer only to documents provided to me by the Prosecution team. Any analysis or conclusions I made were done so on the presumption that any accusations ..." and you use that word. So, General, is that how it was? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was asked to assume that the documents are given -- which were given to me are factually correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to emphasise what you say when you say, "Any analysis or conclusions I made were done so on the presumption of the correctness of all the accusations ..." And that is what you say in paragraph 3. Is that right? Is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: I assume that the state of the procedure is such that the documents put at my disposal are factually correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I understand, yes. I have understood your answer, General. Now, do you happen to know, since you're saying that you drew your conclusions on the assumption that all the accusations were correct, that in modern day law there is a rule or law that is called a presumed innocent, and that is a term that is a basic human right and accepted generally throughout the world?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honours. That is my assumption too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in view of the fact that all your analyses and conclusions were made presuming that all the accusations were correct, that means that you have -- what is done here is starting out from the opposite premise, that is to say the premise of guilt and not the presumption of innocence. Now, this premise of guilt in this part of the world - and when I say "this part of the world" I mean Europe - was last applied during the Inquisition and after that never again. Are you aware of that, General?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These are very broad comments by you, and probably no truth to this at all on any basis. Now, come to a more detailed matter that he can deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, very specifically now, General, is it clear to you, then, that your conclusions, given on the presumption of the correctness of the accusations, that those conclusions then finally should serve as confirmation of those same accusations? Is that clear, that we're in a vicious circle here, a new legal perpetuum mobile, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: As I said before, Your Honour, I do not have any direct experiences. I answered specifically to the questions asked on the basis of the documents I received and my own experience. I did not detail the details of the case, I only examined the possibilities of the functioning of the armies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has made that plain. He's made his position quite clear. Now, let's move on to something else. He's explained his position. If you want some other story, in due course you can give evidence about it. That's his account.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. May, if this isn't clear to you, then fine, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Vegh, in point 17, you say: "During studies of military history, I got an insight into the events of World War II in Yugoslavia." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In the course of my general studies of history, I dealt with World War II. Those were part of my studies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, but you refer to events in Yugoslavia during World War II. Had you said that you dealt with World War II as a whole, I wouldn't have asked you, but you mentioned World War II in Yugoslavia, and I assumed that knowledge served you in writing this report for the opposite side that is bringing you in to testify. Isn't that right, General?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I'm -- I'm talking about general military history.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you know about the events in Yugoslavia during World War II, do you have any knowledge about the genocide against the Serbs that was committed during World War II?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the relevance of all of this, the matter which the witness is giving evidence about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, the witness testified about this and it is contained in paragraph 17. He said, "During my studies of military history, I gained an insight into the events of the Second World War in Yugoslavia." That is what it says in his report. So now I'm asking him that since he is acquainted with Yugoslavia during World War II, whether he knows about the genocide committed during World War II against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's taking up even longer time at the moment. You shall, of course, answer the witness if he wishes, but there are many more matters he deals with. Yes. Let the general answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have knowledge, but I did not get any questions on that in this respect, so I did not deal with it in my report. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Move on to something else. You've heard what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, in paragraph 27 - I'm moving on to another area now - you say that in various -- "In the Yugoslav armed forces eight basic elements are considered important in command and control, and they are: Objectives, authority, responsibility, trust, discipline, morale, regulations and time." Now, where did you get these elements from? What was your source? Because you don't tell us your source in your report. Where do you get the eight elements from?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: The most important elements were mentioned here, and in generally speaking, the regulations of the Yugoslav army were the basis for my choice, but I would like to stress that all these elements are part of any army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, General. Now, speaking about the objectives as the first of those eight elements as you enumerate them, you state the following: "Objectives can be defined as specific values that have to be achieved or preserved. Objectives are determined by social entities or organs. Goals stem from objectives, tasks stem from goals." So what is important for the armed forces, essentially important for the armed forces of Yugoslavia are values which must be preserved, and that represents an objective. For objectives to be put into practice, the armed forces are faced with certain goals; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is correct. Those are goals. On the basis of goals, the tasks of the armies and the strategic goals and the commands are the basis for the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. The tasks of the armed forces of Yugoslavia were provided for in the Yugoslav constitution as the highest legal act in the land; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume, since without doubt you wanted to do the work assigned you well, that you know Article 41, paragraph 1 of the constitution, which speaks about national defence, and I should like to quote that article now. It is the following: "The armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia protect the independence, sovereignty, territorial integrity and by this constitution the social system --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter does not have the document before her. Would the witness proceed slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Speak more slowly, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether this has been translated for the witness, but I was quoting one of the paragraphs from an article in the constitution which states that the armed forces protect the independence, sovereignty, territorial integrity. So I have enumerated those values which the armed forces are there to protect and defend. The goals and the tasks of the armed forces is to protect those values.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't that right, General?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If -- if -- just one moment. If the -- if the witness can answer the question, he can do so, but if it's some account written by the accused, he doesn't have to do that. It's a matter for him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in usual cases, that is how it functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. Therefore, General, we agree that the defence of territorial integrity of a state is something that is a basic constitutionally-provided for task of the armed forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: As far as the strategic goals are not changed, that is natural.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, territorial integrity is a value which is to be protected by the army. I don't assume you challenge that.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: I share this viewpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you -- are you aware of Article 237 of the Yugoslav constitution, which states the following: "It is the inviolable and inalienable right and duty of the people and nations of Yugoslavia, the working people and citizens, to protect and defend the independent sovereignty and territorial integrity ..." et cetera, et cetera. So once again, defence of the same values that the armed forces are there to defend, that is, the inviolable and inalienable right of citizens in general. Isn't that right, General?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Your Honour, generally speaking, that is the task of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, when you compiled your report, did you bear in mind the fact that the Republic of Slovenia and the Republic of Croatia, beginning with mid-1990, so in the middle of 1990, and even earlier, started their preparations and activities that were geared towards their secession?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was not my task in this study to consider this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So you didn't look at that aspect. Now, when you drew up your report, did you have in mind the fact that the Republic of Croatia and its authorities, official ones, began intensively and illegally to arm themselves by importing arms illegally through your own country, in fact, that is to say through Hungary? Did you take that into account when you compiled your report?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Your Honour, since I did not get any questions in this respect, I could not really elaborate in my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you bear in mind, because I assume, General, you must --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given his answer to this. There's no point going on to hear some story that you're trying to prove. It's not fair. Now, find one that the witness can answer, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, he answered my previous question, so how do you know what my next question is going to be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just move on. Let's not waste time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I assume that you collected sufficient information to compile your report, and in doing so did you bear in mind the fact that the authorities of Croatia, the police of Croatia through its special units in places where there was a majority Serb population, launched an action to disarm the police stations forcibly?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, I did not consider this since I did not get any questions in this regard. Only about -- I only answered questions regarding the functioning of the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you are well aware of the fact that there was a conflict going on over there. Isn't that right, General?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes, of course, since the report deals with the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I assume that the conflict has two, and in Bosnia we see three, parties to it. So is it possible to compile a report of this kind by looking at only one side and that in part? As a soldier yourself, do you consider that to be possible?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. My report is relative and is limited to the facts I got. Only the facts and the documents which I got were the basis for my report. As far as the report is perhaps not complete --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the general please repeat this last part of his --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If my report does not appear to be complete, it is because the answers -- the questions were limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you said that you were given questions as to the conduct -- about the conduct of the Serb army. Do you know that at that same time it was the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, and not the Serb army, in actual fact, and that the structure of the command cadres was Yugoslav and not Serb? Of the three military districts that Yugoslavia had, two were led by Croats, had Croats to head them. And in the structure of the General Staff itself, the multi-ethnic principle was applied with a far lesser percentage of the Serbs in the army, and the same was true in the air force and in the navy. So we cannot speak of a Serb army; it was the Yugoslav People's Army. Are you aware of that, General?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes, of course. At the beginning of the conflict, I judged the functioning of the Yugoslav army, and that led to my conclusions about how the Yugoslav army did function and could have functioned at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, in writing your report, did you bear in mind the fact that the Presidency of Yugoslavia on the 9th of January, that is to say at the beginning of 1991 itself, issued an order to disband all irregular armed formations and to have the weapons that were illegally introduced into the country handed over to the authorities or JNA units?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I got documents in this respect and also included them in my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you wrote your report did you bear in mind that on the 20th of January, the Presidency, also in 1991, that is, at the request of the government of the Republic of Croatia extended the deadline for disarmament and the disbanding of irregular formations? And did you bear in mind that that deadline was not respected either?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes. The so-called rogue units are even mentioned in my report. And it -- I also talk about a third appeal. And my conclusion was that the leadership of the Yugoslav army tried to do everything possible in order to have regular activities. Since -- you can see that in point 120. Since the deadline -- since the deadline was not achieved, there were new regulations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you, General, to give me your professional opinion as a competent professional, because the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia, bearing in mind the tense situation in the country and the presence of large quantities of illegally procured weapons, especially in Croatia, so the General Staff appealed to the Presidency as the Supreme Commander with the proposal to raise the level of combat readiness because of the deteriorated political and security situation in the country. So as a soldier yourself, and you were the Chief of the General Staff, do you consider that the General Staff acted properly when, faced with a situation of this kind, it appealed to the Yugoslav state Presidency, that is to say to its Supreme Commander, to issue an order to raise the level of combat readiness because of the situation that prevailed?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. The Supreme Command tried to do everything possible and necessary. At the same time, my conclusion was on the basis of what happened later that the -- in spite of the commands given, it was not possible to have -- to enforce these regulations and commands in each case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your last time before we adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you probably have the wrong information, because I asked you whether the General Staff acted properly what it appealed to the Presidency to raise the level of combat readiness, and the Presidency, as the Supreme Commander, did not authorise that because the representatives of the republics who wished to secede blocked this -- the issuance of this decision by the Presidency, that is to say the army. And I'm asking you as a professional. The army could not act without a Presidency decision, and the Presidency never made that decision or issued that order.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Your Honour, any army takes the steps to maintain combat readiness. This is an army task, a soldier task, and where necessary the leadership has to do everything necessary to maintain the combat readiness of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes. We're grateful for the general to do it, to give his evidence. Would you please be back in 20 minutes, and not to speak, of course, about his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The interpreter in Budapest is in fact a simultaneous interpreter but had been instructed, for administrative reasons, to operate in the way she has been operating. The staff in Budapest tell me they think that the system can now be changed so that she translates simultaneously, offering the possible better use of time. No doubt we must see how it goes. A happy rhythm had developed in the last part, or in the second part of the first session but it may be it can now be done simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's see how we get on. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, you know, because it's in front of you, the report of General Vegh contains 229 [as interpreted] paragraphs, and you know that our time is getting extended even more because we have to wait for interpretation, and you know that I can't finish my cross-examination in two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We of course have that in mind. We'll see if we can deal as awkwardly [sic] as possible. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you know that at the session on the 12th to the 14th of March, 1991, due to political rifts, the Presidency of the SFRY decided to refuse the proposal of the staff of the Supreme Command to raise combat readiness in view of the high amount of illegally imported weapons and international tensions. Do you think that with this refusal of the General Staff proposal the Presidency of the SFRY turned a deaf ear to one of its obligations as prescribed by the constitution and by the law?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honour, that the leadership of the armed forces at the time took the necessary steps that were required in order to maintain all of these activities, and the activities were coherent with the instructions of the political leadership and the expectations of the political leadership as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of this fact, that the political leadership, that is the SFRY Presidency, because of political divisions did not take the decision requested by the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: I'm fully aware of the fact that the highest political leadership had some reshuffling at that level, and as a result of that, I'm going to go into details in my conclusion regarding that new situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. When drawing up the report, did you bear in mind that on the 9th and 10th of May, 1991, the Presidency of the SFRY adopted a specific programme of activities and measures of nine points for a permanent solution to ethnic and nationalist tensions, and one of these proposals was to allow movement only to JNA units and federal police in one of the areas of Croatia populated mostly by Serbs, that is, to restrict movement to all other formations, paramilitary or military?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It will have to be considered again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that -- you mentioned a document in nine points, and I did not have this report in nine points, but I did have a number of documents which defined the internal activities of the armed forces as far as the paramilitary and the protection of the borders are concerned and their cooperation. These documents were available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all right. When preparing your report, did you bear in mind public appeals of both Croatian, Slovene, and Muslim Bosnian authorities and political parties and other similar parties addressed to their compatriots to not join the JNA and not to respond to its call-ups and appeals and even to walk out of the JNA units? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: I did not receive any documents regarding this. And as far as the disciplinary aspects are concerned, I presented in great detail matters of communication in the time of warfare.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, General. Do you know that as early as in May 1991, and we have the example of Split in Croatia, attacks began against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Well, basically, as far as the different missions are concerned, I did not detail them in my report. I'm talking about military manoeuvres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, do you know and did you bear in mind when making your report that after these initial attacks on the JNA, attacks were made not only on officers and not only in barracks but even on their families and property, in their apartments and in the streets, that it became a regular, commonplace occurrence? Did you have information on that?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes. I did have a certain amount of information, and basically as far as the manoeuvres are concerned, I considered a certain part of these manoeuvres as defensive in nature when they concerned the immediate surroundings of the barracks and also living quarters which were in fact under attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But would you agree as a soldier that even without any order or approval from superior places along the chain of command every unit of the JNA in this case is entitled to self-defence if attacked? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: In my opinion, every military organisation requires united control and command, and there has to be a uniform underlying thinking and strategy. So there must be coordination, and I'm aware of this. And I'm perfectly aware of the fact that if the life of a soldier is in danger, then of course he can rightfully use a weapon to defend himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly, because self-defence is acknowledged in international law at all levels. Tell me, General, when making your report, did you also bear in mind that in addition to defending one's own members and property, JNA in Croatia reacted only in a number of other limited cases by acting as a buffer between conflicting parties, that is, between local Croatian forces and Serb formations in order to prevent conflicts on a larger scale? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of this, and my opinion is the following: Every military activity takes place between a higher and lower echelon, and of course the commander is fully responsible whether there is a question of self-defence or any other military activity. So it is the commander's responsibility to follow all the different rules that pertain to the law of war and contacts at wartime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you know that at the time of the adoption of these decisions on the secession of Slovenia and Croatia and the open display of the desire to secede by the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the president of the federal government, that is the Prime Minister, who is a Croat, Ante Markovic, whose government was composed in such a way that all republics and provinces were represented?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: As far as these questions of the leadership are concerned, I've not dealt with these questions, and I have not been asked questions regarding these matters. The only information I have is concerning the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army from Croatia into Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, General. Do you know that this government, the one that I described, on the 26th of June, 1991, evaluated that the decisions of Slovenia and Croatia on secession were illegal, and they were supported in that by the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia, which is the only body entitled to judge the legality and constitutionality of any enactment?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: As far as legal questions are concerned, I did not deal with any of these in my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. Do you know that on the 7th of July, with the participation of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I wonder if we're not going to be wasting a lot of time on this. The general has not been able to give any answers, he's not dealing with it, so what's the point of wasting everybody's time doing it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the point, Mr. May, is that this precedes all the matters that the general deals with, and that is the secession of Croatia and Slovenia. I suppose there is a logical chain of events that enables us to see the whole picture. May I continue with my questions, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will allow, first of all, the witness to see whether there's anything he can add to anything he can add so far on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the events are concerned, I -- I was not asked to study the events prior to the questions that I was asked, so I can only give you concrete answers regarding the facts I've been asked to study.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. As to whether there is any point asking any further questions, it's a matter for the accused, but it doesn't seem to add very much. Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But very briefly, General: You know about the so-called Brioni declaration made with the participation of the representatives European Union, the Presidency of Yugoslavia and representatives of Slovenia and Croatia, which established the presence of the International Monitoring Mission and when it was agreed that the decisions of Slovenia and Croatia on secession be placed under a moratorium. On the 27th of July, a decision was made to introduce an embargo on the use of force, and Slovenia and Croatia made it conditional upon the withdrawal of the army. I suppose you are aware of that.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: I have certain pieces of information. And I would like to assist on the fact that I'm only an expert on military issues, and I have only prepared to answer questions regarding this particular conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the conflict involves two parties, General. You were given certain questions, and you were asked to explain something based on the facts provided you by the opposite side, the conduct of one of these parties, but I suppose there is a causal link --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say page; I said there were two parties to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is a waste of time. We have a detailed description by the witness. What is the point of going through other matters? We've got 200-plus and more. What is the purpose of all this if you don't ask some proper questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I believe I am --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. He was going to respond, the witness. If he wishes, that is, to answer something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, as I said in my report, and I insisted several times, I only studied the conditions of the functioning of the army, the leadership, the control and command, cooperation, discipline, and so on in the first part of my report. And in the second part of my report, I gave answers to concrete questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you should concentrate on the issues of command and control dealt with in the report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But there are also certain things that the witness refers to himself that needs to be elucidated, such as the withdrawal of the army from Croatia and Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, General, that on the 29th of July, 1991, units of the JNA started withdrawing from Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes, of course I know. And a large party of these forces was in fact withdrawn into Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I do discuss this in my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the JNA withdrawal from Croatia was considerably disabled or made impossible precisely by the blockades of the barracks?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I did in fact deal with this question, and I described the fact that the Yugoslav People's Army carried out a very complex, very difficult system of missions. There was a complex task. At the same time, they were withdrawing and they maintained military manoeuvres, and they provided support to the defence forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But in order to understand what was going on at the same time on a parallel track, I will quote just a brief passage from the book of Lord Owen who speaks, for instance, about the Knin Corps, which was an important corps at the time. And you know where the town of Knin is. He writes on page 182 of his book, The Balkan Odyssey, and I'm quoting: "Like other corps, this one was falling apart, too, because officers and troops began declaring themselves as Croats and Slovenes and abandoning the JNA in order to join their own national armies. They left military service, and in some cases, the country. Those, mainly Serbs, who stayed with the JNA did not have any freedom, and many were kept under blockade in barracks by the Croatian army. That is one of the reasons why the JNA reacted so forcefully in places like Vukovar. At that stage a classical, a traditional civil war erupted with breaches of friendships of soldiers within the same corps when they started waging war against one another." I want to ask you, General, did you have in mind the kind of situation described by Lord Owen or did you deal with a different situation as described to you by this side opposite?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes. According to my knowledge, the identity of the armed forces simply stopped at the beginning of the conflict. There was no longer an identity. And also, I know that there was disarmament of certain ethnical groups, and at the same time other groups were armed. And as a result of this, there was an imbalance, there was an uncertainty, and the situation of forces and means changed as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, General. A moment ago, Judge Robinson mentioned command and control. Let us go back, therefore, to objectives as an element essential to command and control in the armed forces of the SFRY. From what I quoted, is it clear that the JNA, which has as a constitutionally defined objective to defend and protect the territorial integrity of the SFRY was facing Croatian forces whose objective was precisely unilateral, forcible secession, i.e., breach of territorial integrity? So you have on the other hand a legal constitutional objective, and on the one hand an objective that is contrary to the constitution. Is that clear, General?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that as far as the Yugoslav army was unified and had unified goals and was intact, this was correct. But after they lost their identity, the strategic goals were different which guided the activities.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the interpreters not to give me the Serb translation while the general is speaking because I'm listening both to the general speaking Hungarian and at the same time the Serbian translation, and I can't understand a thing because I don't speak Hungarian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, is it fair to say that after this refusal from the Presidency to raise combat readiness and to create possibilities for disarming irregular formations the JNA reduced its activities to mere self-defence and, to a lesser extent, calming down inter-ethnic tensions in situations of erupting conflict?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: According to my opinion, the self-defence can only be discussed as regards certain questions. Of course, every military action has goals beyond self-defence; for example, the annihilation of the enemy, the conquering of the territory, and the maintenance of the territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I did not understand this answer completely, but it would take too much time to go through the whole thing again. Do you think, General, since you talk about a shift in objectives, that an armed formation that had been set in a legal way and which instead of its legal objectives and tasks starts carrying out illegal and unconstitutional tasks and objectives becomes in that way illegal and paramilitary? Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Your Honour, according to my opinion, every manoeuvre, every combat at the beginning needs to have a unified command for all military units, and the principle of subordination must prevail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, General. That's not what I asked. I asked you if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's your question? Put it again if you say it's wrong. Let the answer be made if you say it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if an armed formation which instead of its legal objectives and tasks starts carrying out tasks and objectives which are illegal and unconstitutional, does that formation ipso facto become irregular, paramilitary? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes, I understand the question. Such formations, such armed units cannot be allowed. If, however, this should happen, the command has the responsibility to disband these forces or to subordinate them, those semi-military units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your opinion on this matter is of particular interest to me because of the shift in objectives and tasks in the Ministry of Defence of Croatia and Slovenia, because the question arises whether the existence of these formations which used to be legal and constitutional becomes illegal when they started fighting the legal army, the JNA, to achieve forcible secession of Slovenia and Croatia. Is that so or not, General?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: The illegal actions must be prevented at all cost, and only the legal activities -- only legal activities can be allowed for the armed units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, General, do you know that the ZNG, the Croatian National Guard Corps, was formed in May 1991?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: I do know about this, but I did not get any answers to this -- any questions to this respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Since you say that you do know about it, do you also know that the Constitutional Court, when the Croatian National Guards Corps was formed, which was contained in the law enacted by Croatia, and I quote from the decision by the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia. In the law on Croatia, it said: "In the Republic of Croatia, a Croatian National Guards Corps was being established as a professional uniformed armed formation of military set-up for the defence of the country and for keeping law and order as provided for by the Ministry of the Defence of the Republic of Croatia." Now, do you know that, defined in this way, the military structure in Croatia at the time, that is to say in May 1991, was proclaimed by the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia to be unconstitutional and unlawful? So therefore, this was a paramilitary formation; isn't that right, General?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was not my task to deal with the Croatian armed forces and their tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those forces were established before the conflict broke out, and those were the forces that attacked the JNA, that defended itself from them. It was these forces that were paramilitary forces, and pursuant to the decision made by the constitution of Yugoslavia and the position taken by the federal government and these were the forces that stood up to the JNA and opposed it. So all that went before the JNA reactions and the events that I described. And I assume you're bearing that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the witness doesn't want to comment on that he doesn't need to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not wish to comment on this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it might be helpful simply to remind the accused through the Court, and anybody else viewing it, that the general's report was narrowly defined in order, of course, that shouldn't trespass at all on fact-finding functions of the Trial Chamber and shouldn't go beyond the proper remit of an expert. Thus, where he makes any comments on the basis of facts, it's always on the precise basis, assuming facts are as described but making no further comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the accused spends his time for another 25 minutes or so, it may not be much use, but that's his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Precisely so, Your Honour, and of course the report will stand in its conclusions unchallenged by the accused, but that's his choice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand what you're saying, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We've got another quarter of an hour, 20 or minutes or so. We'll give you your time. It's a matter for you how you choose to waste you time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, May. Do you really consider that I can cross-examine this witness based on a report which contains 299 points in the space of two hours with all the technical handicaps that we're witnessing, that we are communicating at a very slow pace today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please concentrate on the issues which are dealt with in the report. Otherwise, we will consider the time you will have for the cross-examination. We will not extend the time for the cross-examination. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in your report, I think that shifting the army and materiel you treat as a planned activity with a strategic goal in mind, and you say that an important part of the JNA was withdrawn from Slovenia and Croatia to strategically important territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina. My question to you is as follows: Isn't it quite obvious that the JNA withdrew from Slovenia and Croatia precisely because those two republics had proclaimed secession and in order to avoid a conflict with the paramilitary formations that were there? And in Croatia, we saw the Vance-Owen Plan come into force, which means that the UN Protection Forces arrived, and they were deployed in the area of Krajina. I assume you're aware of that. So there were agreements reached with the Slovenian and Croatian authorities on that score on the one side and the Presidency of Yugoslavia to have the army leave, both in conformity with the Vance Plan and the agreements reached. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I am aware of that. The 5th Military District units left Croatia and Slovenia, and therefore a strong -- strong concentrations were formed in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the military actions were continued there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In withdrawing from Croatia and Slovenia, parts of the JNA really did reach the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, I assume you'll agree with me there was nothing strange in this because it was Yugoslav territory. It was the state in which the JNA was the official army. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, it was the case, naturally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And apart from that, Bosnia-Herzegovina was closer, territorially speaking, to Croatia and to Slovenia. Serbia, Montenegro, and Macedonia were further away. So it was logical to have a sufficient concentration of forces find itself on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And a considerable portion of the troops going to Serbia went via Bosnia-Herzegovina, or to Montenegro or Macedonia. They had to have found themselves at one point on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and crossing through that territory on their way elsewhere. I assume you know geography. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes, of course. And actually, the withdrawal of the armed forces from the former Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could the general please repeat his answer. Could the general please repeat the answer from "withdrawal."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So after the withdrawal, not only were there strong concentrations of troops, but it is generally known that the strategic reserves of the Yugoslav army, the bases, the air forces and the air defence were partly also in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, because Bosnia-Herzegovina was the centrally located republic of the former Yugoslavia, and Yugoslavia itself always had a plan -- the plan of defending its borders from whatever side they might be attacked, so of course it was normal that it concentrated its largest reserves in that central republic which was furthest from all the borders of the republic itself. I assume you're aware of that, General.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: I also saw the strategic concept like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, when we're talking about the positions of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina, are you aware that in the second half of 1991 already the leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina, without the Serbs albeit, led by Izetbegovic, appealed to the citizens not to respond to calls from the JNA, and even went so far as to ask that all military records be done away with?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Could you please repeat this more slowly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I asked was this: In connection with the position of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina, do you happen to know that the leadership, led by Alija Izetbegovic, already in 1991 called upon the citizens not to respond to the calls from the JNA and asked that all military records be done away with, removed.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: I did not receive any documents to this respect. They were not at my disposal. I know the Yugoslav army's doctrine in this respect and the questions pertaining to doctrine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you, General, as I assume that you're putting the pieces of a puzzle together, are you aware of the existence in Bosnia-Herzegovina paramilitary organisations that were called the Patriotic League, which was established by Izetbegovic and even to the present day that 31st of March, 1991, that particular date - and let me emphasise the year, 1991 - that is to say one year before the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that it is officially celebrated as the day on which the Patriotic League was formed and it's celebrated as Patriotic League Day. So do you know that this took place one year before the conflict actually broke out? The Muslim side established this paramilitary formation that was called the Patriotic League, and prior to the conflict it numbered more than 100.000 armed men.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- my task was only to deal with the doctrine and the tasks of the Yugoslav People's Army. I did not consider the things which the witness [as interpreted] talks about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all these organisations, those which attacked the Yugoslav People's Army and were placed in the role of forcible secession, were not your assignment. You weren't asked to look at them, were you, General?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you at least know this: That before the war officially began in Bosnia-Herzegovina, tens of Serbs had been killed without any cause?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I simply don't understand how this is helping the Chamber. It's wasting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I agree. We haven't stopped him in order to try and not waste further time. He must be allowed a reasonable time but it doesn't seem to add very much. The witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It seems so regrettable and the very considerable resources of the Tribunal in making this excellent videolink available from Budapest are frankly wasted in this way and the general's time is wasted as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's had the opportunity to give the evidence. We are very grateful to him. Whether the accused asks anything is a totally different matter. Yes. Let's move on to something else. Are you going to ask him any questions, for instance, instead of talking?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am constantly asking him questions, and the general's answers were that that wasn't the assignment he was given by the opposite side, so I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's a complete waste of time, waste for everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, is it true that the army in Bosnia-Herzegovina was established on the 15th of April, 1992? Officially.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
