utterances.text: Very well. And the army of Republika Srpska was established one month later, that is to say on the 15th of May, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your report, you refer to some sort of transition by the JNA into the army of Republika Srpska, and this is a title on page 10 of the second part of your report. And from the text, it appears that there was a special plan to create the army of Republika Srpska from a part of the JNA, if I've understood your report correctly.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: I think that in 1992, in the spring of 1992, in May, there was a very complicated reorganisation. There was a time when the army withdrew, and when the army had withdrawn, a new military -- the -- the army continued their activities in a new district and that is how, in my opinion, the possibility of the formation of a new military force arose.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the general please repeat the last part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. If you would repeat that again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the withdrawal of the armed forces, a new army unit was created. And the withdrawal of certain units of the Yugoslav army was made possible, and the circumstances for the achievement of the strategic goals were made possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, that seems to me to be rather generalised. Now, do you know that when the secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina took place in Skopje 26th of April, 1992, a meeting was held by the vice-president of the Yugoslav state Presidency, Branko Kostic, General Colonel Blagoje Adzic, who was chief of the General Staff, and the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, and at that meeting it was agreed that in -- that the competent authorities of the JNA and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina would as soon as possible reach an agreement with respect to the status of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there was talk of a time limit, a deadline by which the JNA should withdraw from Bosnia-Herzegovina and for its transformation as well. In conformity with that, the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes. On 19th May of 1992 the Yugoslavian army withdrew the forces which were not necessary there. At the same time, before that, the Yugoslav army -- from part of the Yugoslav army, the Bosnian Herzegovina army was formed. The army of the Yugoslav Republic had officers and troops in many -- which were resident in many different places, and those which were locals remained. And it is probable that technical material also remained in place, considerable technical material, equipment and also it is probable that those newly formed units were supported with logistics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, General, please. Doesn't it seem to you to be logical that if Bosnia-Herzegovina are -- is becoming gradually independent and establishing itself as a new state, that the citizens from the territory of that new state are preparing to live and work in that state and be citizens of that state? And if they are by profession soldiers, for example, then they will continue to perform that profession in the state whose citizens they are? Do you know that the composition of the army of Republika Srpska was made up from people of Bosnia-Herzegovina? They were all citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in fact. They weren't members of the JNA who had come in from Serbia, for example, or Macedonia, Montenegro; they were already citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes. And since the new forces had a great many troops, naturally part of the army was composed of those people. And at the same time, the documents made available to me prove that the JNA had a number of officers and sub-officers who remained in place and who participated in bringing about the new forces and continued serving in the new army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vegh, the JNA didn't leave them. The people who were from Bosnia-Herzegovina remained in their own republic. And the army of Yugoslavia, because the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia made up of Serbia and Montenegro was formed, withdrew its citizens. So how can the army of Yugoslavia withdrew -- withdraw citizens from another state from that territory? For what reason? Why would it do that?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: In my opinion, this was a process of reorganisation which was extremely complex, and in fact for the 2nd Military District, became the base for the new Bosnian armed forces. And as far as planning and organisation was concerned, that required knowledge and expertise and know-how, and the Yugoslav People's Army ex-officers became members of the new force precisely in order to help its successful functioning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They remained in their republic. General, please, on the 4th of May, 1992, that is to say before the official withdrawal, so I'm talking about the 4th of May, the Yugoslav state Presidency officially called upon the leadership of the three ethnicities in Bosnia-Herzegovina to decide about taking over the JNA whose military composition was made up of the citizens of that republic. And the official announcement made was that the Yugoslav state Presidency at its session made a decision for the accelerated withdrawal from Bosnia-Herzegovina of all citizens of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia who find themselves in service in the JNA in that republic. In view of the fact that the process will be completed within 15 days at the latest, according to the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, there are no more grounds for the Presidency of Yugoslavia or any other body of Yugoslavia decide on military matters on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Presidency of Yugoslavia appeals to the leadership --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. The witness must have a chance to deal with this. Would you deal with these fairly slowly. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I want to read this out: "The Presidency of Yugoslavia appeals to the leadership of the three ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say the Muslims, Serbs, and Croats, to agree amongst themselves and to decide upon taking over the JNA whose military composition was made up of the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to avoid any unfortunate situations and consequences." So what else could the Yugoslav state Presidency have done? Faced with the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it withdrew its citizens to the -- its territory and left the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina on their own territory.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: I have no doubt as to such measures which took place, but on the basis of the documents that I received, the Yugoslav People's Army left a number of officers, NCOs, and troops that remained in place and continued serving in the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, similarly, the officers and soldiers of the Yugoslav People's Army made up the fulcrum of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the army of Croatia, the backbone, because there were no others because this division came about. Isn't at that clear, General?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: I have no doubts about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, since you say that you were supplied with documents relating to the events linked to this withdrawal, I should like to remind you, and I assume you have had occasion to see this for yourself, the report by the UN Secretary-General dated the 30th of May, 1992, on the application of the UN Security Council Resolution 752. And I shall, just in brief terms, or very briefly, quote from that because it deviates from what the other side showed you as documents, this report by the UN Secretary-General. I'm just going to quote several passages from the original Resolution. Point 5: "[In English] The bulk of the JNA personnel who were deployed in Bosnia and Herzegovina were citizens of that republic and were not, therefore, covered by the Belgrade authorities' decision of 4th of May to withdraw JNA from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Most of them appear to have joined the army of so-called Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Others have joined the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is under the political control of the Presidency of that republic. Others may have joined various irregular forces operating there. Those who are not citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina are said by the Belgrade authorities to number barely 20 per cent of the total. Most of these are believed to have withdrawn already into Serbia and Montenegro, some of them having been subjected to attack during their withdrawal. Others, however, remain at various garrisons in Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially in Serb-controlled areas, including two installations on the outskirts of Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You must let the witness answer, if he wants to. Is there anything you would like to add to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just wait.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me finish the quotation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, but very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "[In English] A further category consists of personnel --" [Interpretation] That is the preceding category, the second one, about which it is said that they remained on the edges of Sarajevo. "A further category remains in Sarajevo who had been blockaded in their barracks by the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina or hostile irregular forces." So I'm quoting Boutros Boutros-Ghali here, report of the UN Secretary-General of 1992, the 30th of May, 1992. Do you understand, General, that this runs counter to the conclusions that you drew?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Your Honour, in -- in my opinion, the Serbian army in Bosnia was supposed to protect the territory with the reservists in place. They had to pull them into the army and also include members of the population. Paramilitary units could also join them in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, go on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much time do I have left, Mr. Kwon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The answer is that at the moment you have another 20 -- 20 minutes or so. We will continue. Whether you get any extra minutes, it won't be very many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: After the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you then, General, about what the UN Secretary-General said, namely that the JNA withdrew from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Look at what it says in the same report about the presence of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Ghali says: "[In English] Regarding the withdrawal of elements of the Croatian army in Bosnia, information currently available in New York suggests that no such withdrawal has occurred. UNPROFOR has received reliable reports of Croatian army personnel in uniform operating within as part of military formation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Croatian authorities have consistently taken position, consistently taken position that the Croatian soldiers in Bosnia and Herzegovina have left the Croatian army and are not subject to this authority. International observers do not, however -- do not, however, doubt that portions of Bosnia and Herzegovina are under control of Croatian military units, whether belonging to the local Territorial Defence, to paramilitary groups, or to the Croatian army. It is unclear in the circumstances how their withdrawal or disbandment, as required by the Council, can be achieved." [Interpretation] So you don't deal with this in your report. As you see, the report of the UN Secretary-General points to the decision of Yugoslavia to withdraw its own citizens, not other countries' citizens, as well as the fact that the Croatian army is not withdrawing from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you have any comment upon this, General?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt the reality of this particular report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. So as a result of the agreement of the Presidency of the SFRY, which took on the 4th of May the decision to withdraw the JNA, which Boutros-Ghali refers to in his report, that is, with a proviso that members of the JNA who are not locals of Bosnia and Herzegovina had to withdraw, and people who were born in Bosnia-Herzegovina were allowed to stay, but not as members of the JNA because the JNA no longer existed in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Your Honour, after the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA was transformed and it became the military forces of Yugoslavia. But at the same time, the people who were living in this area joined the Bosnian People's Army. But according to reports, we know that these people nevertheless continued to receive their supplies and their pay from the Yugoslav People's Army, and also in legal matters was also part and parcel of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in Republika Srpska, on the 15th of May, the army of Republika Srpska was established and some, of course not all, former JNA members from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina joined that army. Among others, its commander, General Ratko Mladic, who was also a local of Bosnia-Herzegovina, unlike, for instance, the Chief of Staff of the VRS at the time, Sefer Halilovic, who was from Serbia but who had come to Bosnia-Herzegovina to fight in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. If we were to look strictly at who came from where, then Serbia could be accused of sending Sefer Halilovic to Bosnia-Herzegovina to organise the defence of Bosnia. I suppose you know all this, General.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my opinion, these officers and NCOs from the material point of view, from the point of view of personnel issues and material question, were still part of their original organisation, and this was proven by the fact that promotions, pensions, and other financial issues, they were still addressing the leadership of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's quite another matter, and we shouldn't waste time on it. It's the question of assistance. Is it in issue, General, that the VRS fought for the protection and equality of its own people in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Everybody had the right to self-defence. I suppose that includes Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes. Naturally, this is what the doctrine expresses and contains.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know full well that Serbs accepted the so-called Cutileiro plan which divided Bosnia and Herzegovina into cantons and that its implementation could have prevented the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina but it was refused by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it really is absurd for the accused to try and put in his case through a witness who has come here to do one thing and has researched one thing and by asking questions that he may know a little about, he may know something about, but his answers to which are unlikely to be regarded as determinative by the Court when these are matters that the Court has to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm a fervent believer in the right to cross-examine, and I have supported consistently your right to cross-examine, but on this occasion you are abusing it, and I regret to say I will not be in a position to support an extension.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, General, that after the agreement on withdrawal from Bosnia and Herzegovina was reached Muslim forces interfered with that withdrawal and hampered it by armed attacks? The most notorious is the attack on the withdrawing column of the army in the Dobrovoljacka Street in Sarajevo. I suppose you know that.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes, there might have been such atrocities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 15th of May in Tuzla, also during the evacuation of the JNA from the Husinska Buna barracks, a JNA column was ambushed? People were burning like torches, and the JNA was very peacefully withdrawing from their barracks in Tuzla. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes. It might have taken place, but I have no knowledge of concrete events that have taken place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Ghali's report that I quoted, it says, among other things: "The Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina had initially been reluctant to engage in talks [In English] on these and other issues with the leadership of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. A senior JNA representative from Belgrade, General Nedeljko Boskovic, has conducted discussions with the Bosnia and Herzegovina Presidency, but it has become clear that his word is not binding on the commander of the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." [Interpretation] Do we see from here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, your time is coming up. You can ask, given the time that has been wasted, you can ask one final question now and then it will be brought to an end.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought you would give me at least those 20 minutes that Mr. Kwon mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We're not going to on this occasion because of the time you've wasted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let us elucidate one more thing: Paragraph 296, towards the end of your report --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm quoting you: "In my opinion, as far as command and control are concerned, two completely independent armed forces came into being which contained new order of battle elements at different organisations and different sets of missions." Is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, naturally.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And just one more thing I would like to clarify, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, one more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You proceed, General, from the premise that the army of Yugoslavia waged war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you draw your conclusions from some Drina Operation or a Gvozd Operation, whereas neither operation, Drina or Gvozd - and I must say I received the Drina plan from a previous witness - contain no elements of any planning on the part of the army of Yugoslavia. They are documents of the VRS. And even as such, as documents of the VRS, they were never implemented because they deal with the situation in which they would be attacked. But the army of the VRS -- sorry, the army of Yugoslavia did not respond, even when it was attacked in the Flash Operation or the Storm Operation. Nor was the Gvozd Operation plan implemented. And you know that staffs prepare different plans for different eventualities. Do you know that this plan that was never realised is exclusively a plan of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must bring this to a question. What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my duty was to give my opinion concerning the plan, and this is exactly what I did. Now, as far as the implementation of the plan and the way it actually was carried out, these are things that I had not been asked to comment on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn. Now, how long do you think you might be?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very, very brief on the one army issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Then we will allow the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I should be very brief in re-examination and I'm hopeful that we conclude Mr. Theunens today, given that there's five days between -- four days between now and when we next sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider the position today. It's a question of time. General, thank you for your assistance, but there will be another 20 minutes or so. We will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Questioned by Mr. Kay:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Vegh, you recognise that the VRS and VJ became two separate armed forces. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes. After the withdrawal, that was correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the features that, therefore, is recognised by you is that there then came about a separate command and control system of each armed forces.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes. Separate -- there were separate systems of commands, although there was close cooperation between the forces in carrying out their tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this separation, the VRS then became an armed force that was able to act independently and separately from the VJ.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes. It was an independent military force, in my opinion, which had also independent tasks to comply with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was able to undertake its own operations of a military nature that were independent of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: In my opinion, that -- they only had limited possibility of military actions. They needed logistic and combat support.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One factor within your report that I would like to ask you about, which is one that has not been considered, and it arises from the original existence of there being one force, the JNA, and then the division into the VJ and VRS, and that concerns the already existing links between the military leaders. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Before the withdrawal, the Yugoslav People's Army was independent. After the forming of the Bosnian army, it was divided into two armed forces, and they were able to carry out their tasks independently from each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Mladic, who became the commander of the VRS armed forces, had good links of a personal nature with officers within the VJ. Is that something that was within the information that was given to you or something that you were aware of when drafting your report?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes, it was contained in the informations, in the personal reports. I got documents about his new post and about his activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Mladic had been a very popular figure within the army of the JNA and was able to take those links and that popularity with him into the VRS. Is that something that you were able to recognise?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: I think that the general had official and unofficial links with the Yugoslav army which he continued to have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The last matter you raised there is that which I was going to deal with next, that he was able to rely upon those pre-existing ties and links to draw on resources for the VRS for his own command and control.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: I think that the appointment of the general was on the recommendation of the Yugoslav army in consideration of his experiences. He knew about the doctrine, and he relied on the traditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few matters in re-examination. Re-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your overall opinion on the degree of separateness or the character of separateness of the two armies is set out in full in the last paragraphs of your report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Could you please repeat this? The answer is yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Immediately before that, in dealing with one particular document at the request of the OTP, you reviewed the 50th Sessions of the national Assembly of the Republika Srpska and the document recording what was said at that session about the level of support for the VRS from the VJ.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes. I reviewed this document, especially as far as the ammunition supply was concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that level of support, as you understand it to have been, find reflection in your answer about the limited ability of the VRS to carry out independent military operations?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes. I think that the VRS had only very limited material possibilities and was forced to have continuous support by the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On an associated point, not exactly parallel but associated, at paragraph 194 of your report you express the view that in cases of assignment of personnel from one force to another to perform military duty, responsibility for disciplinary matters of the assigned personnel stays with the assigning force. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Yes. When a soldier or troops are subordinated to another unit, only the -- only the command is transferred. The personnel and the disciplinary questions remain with the original commander if the regulation does not foresee otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that a general finding or is it specifically related to the situation in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that His Honour Judge Robinson would like to know whether this is a general finding. You said yes, but I'm not quite sure whether you're saying yes to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think he was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a general observation, but the constitution makes the fine points on it, so to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was the situation in Yugoslavia? I mean, are you in a position -- are you in a position to say that that general finding applied in the specific situation of Yugoslavia, that responsibility remained with the assigning force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is generally so, and I assume that it also is so in the case given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You assume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The -- this is what the military rules prescribe. It is general practice when troops or soldiers are assigned to another unit or force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, General, on both the question of the consequences in law for support by one army for another, that's the ammunition and so on, or assignment of troops, these questions are questions outside your area of expertise and matters ultimately for the Judges or not?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: I think that, generally speaking, it does belong to my province, and this is not an extraordinary case. And the regulation also applies to all NATO countries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a couple more questions. Drina and Gvozd as proposed operations, to set out these plans, what level of authority would have been required; top level, mid-level, or where?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Generally speaking, such plans are always drawn up by the strategic leaders. That means the Defence Ministry and the political leadership approves those plans and the -- and the strategic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the general please repeat what he said after "the Defence Ministry."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The strategic plans are drawn up on the leadership level, and the political leadership approves. The war plans are also drawn up on the highest military level involving the commanders who would participate. The combat plans are drawn up by the mid-level leadership, so on the mid-level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Drina plan, it is said, never came into effect. That's not the point of the questions you've been asked about it. As planned, did it involve a substantial contribution from the VJ?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: I did not quite understand this question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Drina plan -- you remember dealing with the Drina plan in your report. The suggestion by the accused has been that it didn't actually take place. The point is, as planned, did the Drina plan foresee substantial activity by the VJ in cooperation with the VRS?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: I think that each approved plan must be started according to the approved points. Of course, the plans may change as required, but also for those changes, approval of the leadership is required.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked a question about the forces in Croatia at the beginning of the conflict and at the time of the separation, and I think the word "paramilitary" was used in the description of those forces. It matters not to us at all what term is applied, but if the term "paramilitary" was appropriate to the forces in Croatia at the beginning of the conflict, is the same term appropriate to the VRS and the SVK?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Of course those paramilitary units might have been operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've made the point, Your Honour, and I'm going to move on to save time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked about events in Croatia on a particular basis by the accused. Were you -- are you aware of events in August 1990 where Martic took possession of the Knin police station?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Could -- could you please -- could you please repeat what you said after "August 1990."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Martic took possession of the Knin place station.

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the whole question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, for want of time I'm going to move on. In any event, this was questioning of the witness outside the area of his expertise, and I don't think it's necessary to go further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then finally as to your report, you were asked a large number of questions about the basis of your report and the suggestion being that you had in some way not taken account of the other side to a conflict or the other sides to a conflict. Was it any part of your report to examine the conflict overall or were you concerned, as instructed, simply to look at the development of the JNA, the VJ, the VRS, and the SVK, and to look at their interrelations one to another?

utterances.speaker: FERENC VEGH
utterances.text: I examined the situation in a general way based on the documents, and that was the basis for my conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's all I need ask, I think. With many thanks to the general for his assistance but also, if I may, through the Chamber, to the authorities, I think the military authorities in Budapest, which have made available the videolink facility which, as we've seen, is of a particularly high quality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's certainly right, and we're very grateful to the general to be here to assist us today, and we thank him for his assistance, and we now bring that to an end. Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the transmission can end, then the next -- we return to the evidence of Reynaud Theunens. He is, I hope, outside the door, so that we can maximise the use of time today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We may not be able to finish it in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll hope for the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the witness enters the courtroom, I have something to say with respect to the list of witnesses, and as there is a protected witness, I assume we ought to go into private session just for a second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes you have now, Mr. Milosevic, so you need to organise your own time, but you have no more.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, you said yesterday that I would have 50 minutes, now you say I have 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Fifteen. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, the JNA was present in Croatia up until the Vance-Owen Plan came into force; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not the Vance-Owen Plan, it's the Vance Plan. The Vance Plan was a transitional solution consisting of various aspects, one of the aspects being the withdrawal of the armed forces, the JNA and the Croatian counterpart, as well as the demilitarisation of the existing forces in the area, being the local Serb TO. Now, I didn't focus my analysis on that aspect, but you will find in the second part of the document, and if there is further detail noted, I can provide you with the exact page numbers. There are JNA documents dealing, for example, with the transfer of JNA units into local Serb TO units. There are also documents included in the section on logistical support dealing with the creation of a logistical infrastructure for the RSK TO, and subsequently the SVK, in a way to have a solution for when the JNA isn't there any more. This is also linked to the issue we discussed earlier, namely the provision of personnel from the JNA to the local Serb defence structures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I didn't say the Vance-Owen Plan, I said the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the transcript reads on my monitor Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the transcript can make a mistake. I cannot. Is it common knowledge, Mr. Theunens, that -- when we're talking about the plan, of course, because I always strode to have it adopted and I do know that it was, that it was Vance's plan, I hope you don't challenge that from the moment the forces of the United Nations placed under their protection these zones, these territories, Croatian territory was not attacked from those zones until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, my report doesn't deal with the activities of the Croatian armed forces related to the UNPAs or not. Now, if required, I can provide an answer based on my experience when serving in UNPROFOR. It may well be correct that there were no offensive operations or major offensive operations launched by the local Serb forces from the UNPAs, but I do recall that there were regular exchanges of small-arms fire, mortar, or even artillery between both warring factions, so as well the Croatian armed forces as the local Serb armed forces, HV and SVK, along the separation line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, do you know on the basis of documents and the actual state of affairs as it was that the armed forces of Krajina surrendered all heavy weapons according to the double-key formula, one to them and one to the UN, handed over to UNPROFOR? Is that right, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, this is not part of my analysis. If required, I can provide an answer based on my experience both in UNPROFOR and earlier when working with the Belgium Ministry of Defence. This experience is then focused on the situation in Sector East where Belgium had one battalion deployed in Baranja. It may well be correct that initially the weapons were surrendered and put under a double key system, so a key for the local Serb armed forces and UNPROFOR in a number of weapons storage areas, however, quite shortly afterwards, for a number of reasons, weapons were taken back, and I don't recall an exact date when weapons were taken back. They were actually taken back several times and returned and taken back again, but between let's say the latter part of 1992 and 1995. And for example, when I was working in the UNPROFOR headquarters between November -- excuse me, December 1994 and October 1995, we carried out a number of visits to not only to Sector East, so the eastern part of Croatia, but also other areas including Sector North and Sector West, and during these visits, even if our freedom of movement was significantly limited by not only local Serb armed forces, I have to include also the Croatian armed forces, but notwithstanding these limitations, we could notice ourselves that weapons, tanks, guns, were deployed along the separation zone. So this initial situation of withdrawal of weapons and putting them under a double-key system was only an initial situation which didn't last.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't you think that it is very vital that it went on up until the time that the Croatian forces attacked the protected areas? And then they had to take up weapons again to defend themselves. Are you aware of that? Do you know about it? They surrendered their weapons, it was under the double-key system, they were then attacked and had to take up arms again to defend themselves. Was that how it was or not, Mr. Thuenens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, based --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just give me a yes or no answer, please. You needn't go into lengthy explanations.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. If your answer is no, then I'm going to read -- the 30th of June, 1992 is the date, it is a UN Security Council document, so I'm not reading the papers to you, it is the UN Security Council in New York, adopted Resolution 762, which calls on the Croatian government to hand back the pink zones to UN control, and Croatia was condemned for the offensive on the 21st of June and the bombing of Knin and they were threatened with sanctions should they not comply with the demands set out in this Resolution. Is that right, Mr. Theunens? You looked at the documents, you're a military analyst yourself. Is that correct or perhaps this is some sort of fiction too, this UN Security Council Resolution.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, my answer will consist of two parts. First of all, my report did not include an analysis of the I think over hundred -- 100 Security Council Resolutions that were adopted between end of 1991 and mid of 1995 related to the conflict in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Secondly, the question or actually the comment put by Mr. Milosevic is, according to my experience, an incorrect reflection of the facts. Resolution 762 dated indeed from 30th of June, 1992, but what I tried to explain in my -- in the answer to your previous question was that actually a lot of events occurred or happened between the 30th of June, 1992, and the 1st Croatian -- the first significant Croatian military operation against RSK-held territory, namely Operation Flash which was launched early May 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So before May 1995, there were no operations against the protected areas. Is that what you're saying, Mr. Theunens, on the basis of the facts you have at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that's not what I'm saying because I spoke about the first significant Croatian military operation. I am aware of the operation against the Medak pocket which took place -- which was launched, if I'm correct, around early September 1993. And at that time too the United Nations adopted a Resolution urging Croatia to withdraw troops. I also recall that around that time - and I recall that not from my work in the OTP but from my activities prior to my taking up a position here at the OTP - that in September 1993 as a -- as a reprisal, the local Serb armed forces tried to or attempted to shell, for example, Croatian cities with long range artillery and there was, for example, ECMM reporting, so the European Commission Monitoring Mission, that a kind of rocket or even a rocket had impacted close to its hotel on the southern borders of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Theunens. As my time is limited, these are the facts, the material facts that cannot be disputed.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends which facts you want to raise, Mr. Milosevic -- or, Your Honours, especially when it concerns facts related to the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, in your report you say that there was a letter by Helsinki Watch, and it spoke about various things. It mentioned the media, and it mentioned crimes in that range. And on page 134 of the report, of your report, you talk about the response to that letter. It was addressed to me, I think, as well. I just pulled out this piece of paper from the whole document, but it says here that the letter was addressed to me, and then you say, "The chef de cabinet of Slobodan Milosevic, Goran Milicevic, sent the Helsinki Watch organisation the following response," and then you have the response sent by my chef de cabinet, which reads as follows: "In connection with the letter sent on the 21st of January to the president of the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Slobodan Milosevic by the US Helsinki Watch committee, we should like to inform you of the following: First, the places in which the mentioned crimes were made -- were perpetrated are not located within the territory of the Republic of Serbia." So in -- that letter obviously makes mention of certain locations where crimes had been committed. And it goes on to say, "Therefore, this republic is not competent or in any way involved in acts of that kind, and in this connection, the Republic of Serbia cannot be held responsible for those acts. "Point 2: The president of the Republic of Serbia has asked the competent authorities in the Republic of Serbia to investigate the violations that you stipulate in your letter, and if any citizen of the Republic of Serbia took part in the perpetration of those crimes, he will be prosecuted and brought to justice." Now, tell me, please, what is there in that letter which is not logical or incorrect? And one more question, let me add to that, do you know that the first trials for war crimes, when it came to citizens of Serbia that were committed somewhere outside Serbia, were court cases that were tried in Serbia itself. Is that something that you know about?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe Mr. Milosevic is referring to the letter which has been exhibited already. It's Exhibit 359, tab 6. Now, when you look at my report on the page when --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's your document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When you look at the page in my report, it's page 130 of the second part where this letter is discussed. I only quote the letter. There is no analysis or conclusion or anything else related to that letter. Now, to answer the second question of Mr. Milosevic, I also quote another Human Rights Watch publication, and this starts on page 134 of the second part of the report. It's a Human Rights Watch Helsinki report published in July 1995, entitled War Crimes Trials in the Former Yugoslavia. And without going into detail, I think the article indeed refers to a trial that was ongoing, and from other -- from open sources, local open sources, I believe this may be a trial that is related to the activities of so-called Yellow Wasps, another paramilitary group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Has 15 minutes gone by already? Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just clear one more matter up, then. You said that in Yugoslavia, officers who had committed certain crimes were even promoted, and you gave as an example, the name of Colonel Sljivancanin in that respect. Tell me now, please, Mr. Theunens, do you know that with respect to this alleged guilt and the indictments and accusations made against Colonel Sljivancanin, that there were proceedings before the military court in Belgrade, that Colonel Sljivancanin was heard and examined by the court, as were other individuals, and that the military court in Belgrade or, rather, the competent authorities of military legislation reached the conclusion that Colonel Sljivancanin was not guilty of having committed any crimes? And this will be proved. Sljivancanin, unfortunately, is here, but he is an honourable officer who did not commit any crimes, and this was noted. So what do you expect, except for the fact that the allegations made in an accusation be scrutinised to see whether they are true and then they were rejected, and the man is innocent.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to correct what Mr. Milosevic said, or at least the transcript, then. My report does not say that Colonel Sljivancanin committed certain crimes. My report on page 139, paragraph D - so it's the second part of the report again - mentions officer who had been indicted by the ICTY. Now, I think that's clear enough. It doesn't mean that -- it doesn't mean that I wrote it that he has committed certain crimes. Now, I can only say, and that's reflected in this particular paragraph, that Major -- excuse me, Colonel Sljivancanin had been indicted for war crimes I think end of November 1995, and that did not prevent him from pursuing or continuing his military career, achieving senior ranks, and even being admitted to the most senior military courses, staff courses in FRY. I am familiar with the Belgrade military court case of 1998. And actually, yeah, Mr. Milosevic himself mentioned that Sljivancanin is here now, and that's all I have to say about this aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I was really hesitant as to which topic to choose for my examination of Mr. Theunens. I finally decided on paragraph 5 of his expert report, the armed forces of SFRY and the conflict in Croatia. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, in paragraph 5, in the first sentence you said that republican presidents were not part of the Supreme Command and had no legal competencies over the Yugoslav People's Army. I am particularly interested in the year 1991 and in the entire period until the Presidency existed, even if it was only the rump one. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, could Mr. Tapuskovic repeat which paragraph he's referring to, because my paragraph 5 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of the executive summary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the executive summary. Okay. Well, indeed, according to the legal framework or the laws I looked at, namely the 1974 constitution and the 1982 Law on All People's Defence, there is no role for the republican presidents, or no part for the republican presidents in the command or the Supreme Command. The Supreme Command consists of the Presidency, so the representatives of the republics and autonomous provinces, according to the law, and is assisted by a Supreme Command staff consisting of the Federal Secretary for People's Defence, his secretariat, and the Chief of General Staff and the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please look at paragraph 7 of the executive summary. You explained this already yesterday, but I would like to come back to this issue, because it remained unclear, and I would like to clarify it for the Judges. Is it clear that you haven't come across a single order that pertains to any orders given by the JNA to the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have attempted to explain over the past days that paramilitaries was used in two conditions. It was used to identify the enemy forces, and in the second instance -- or it was also used to identify -- it was used by security organs or other security or intelligence organisations investigating volunteer groups. As paramilitary groups were not foreseen in the legal framework, I think it is quite logical that JNA orders of that time would not include the name "paramilitaries," because if they did, then the order would be illegal. So therefore - and I think that was clear from the documents we looked at - the name, or the description of "volunteers" was used. Like, for example, we saw the war diaries of the Guards Brigade where there is mentioning of Seselj's volunteers, or the name Territorial Defence Detachment was used, for example, the Vukovar TO. When you look at the second part of the report and where the operations in Eastern Slavonia --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You say here in the first sentence of paragraph 7, you say: "In order to regularise the de facto situation that existed on the ground in particular with regard to the presence of volunteer groups and paramilitary formations, legislation was amended." And here you speak of the period of August and September 1991.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you dealt with these matters regarding the paramilitaries, you mentioned Kadijevic's book. Kadijevic's book was not exhibited in these proceedings, but it was mentioned several times. You yourself referred to it. But it is -- but there is another document which has been exhibited and concerns the paramilitaries, and I would like it shown to you now so that you explain to the Judges whether you were aware of it. While you were doing your work, have you been shown this exhibit which is 328, tab 18?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I referred to it several times, Your Honours, but the expert who is now before us is somebody who could give us a qualified opinion on it. I have it here in English, and I marked the pages I would like to show to him. It's only several passages.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the tab number again?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 16. It concerns the meeting of the Presidency with the top leadership of the military at the most critical moment, and it concerns the paramilitaries. I would like the expert to look at the English version, page 34, paragraphs 2 to 6, where Kadijevic speaks for the record about certain things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before? These are minutes, in fact.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I -- I'm -- I cannot recall whether I recognise the document now. I would like to make a correction. I used Kadijevic's book only or mainly -- I read the whole book, obviously, but I was mainly to explain the evolution in the objectives of the SFRY armed forces. It was not myself who brought --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I don't need Kadijevic's book. I'm showing you a document and what Kadijevic said, according to stenographic notes, to the political leadership of the state. Look at page 34, paragraphs 2 to 6. He was speaking about the compositions of armed forces which numbered up to 200.000 people, whereas the army of Yugoslavia had less than 100.000.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The first number refers to irregular forces, irregular armed forces.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would still like to finish my previous answer. It is that I didn't bring up Kadijevic's book to discuss the issue of paramilitaries. I used Kadijevic's book mainly to obtain an understanding of the evolution in the operations of the JNA and, more specifically, the mission of the SFRY armed forces during the conflict in Croatia as Kadijevic in his position of Federal Secretariat for People's Defence was one of the best placed people to discuss that issue. As far as these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, stop interrupting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as these figures are concerned, it's a bit difficult to comment on them in a sense that I haven't analysed this document before, I can't compare it with other sources. I know from experience that when armed forces discuss the opposing forces, sometimes at least in -- not only in the former Yugoslavia but also in other situations they can be quite generous when they have to make assessments on the strength and the capabilities of the enemy, for various reasons, so I would prefer not to comment on this particular document, or at least not on this particular passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The final question, please, today, before we go on to another day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't understand. I'm trying to complete this with only two more questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at page 140 in the English version, paragraph 2, where Kadijevic said at that gathering: "We believe that the paragraph 1 and especially the demobilisation of irregular organisations are a key point for peace in Yugoslavia. We are not insisting on other things. But we have to insist on this, I believe, because it is the basic condition for peace in Yugoslavia. Demobilisation of all paramilitary units. And Mesic responded when the decision was almost made: 'You make the decision, but I won't sign it.'" All this is in this document. Do you know about this or not? And how is it possible that you did not receive this document from the OTP when you made your analysis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The last question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- my -- I didn't say that I didn't receive the document, I only said that I don't recall seeing it now. There are 400 footnotes or 400 -- at least 400 documents have been included in the report itself. It's obvious that myself and my colleague Borrelli, who assisted me with the Bosnia-Herzegovina report, also looked at many documents and we had to make choices. So I don't claim that I didn't receive the document. As far as these statements are concerned, again, I do recall that the situation of SFRY Presidency around July 1991 time -- time period was quite complicated. I can comment on Kadijevic's passage and say, yes, indeed, it would probably have helped if all paramilitaries or even -- if all paramilitaries had been demobilised or disarmed and the military adopted a more peaceful stance, but in general, the military does what the political leadership tells it. So I assume there's also responsibility for the political leadership on that level. And I'm not a political analyst, I'm employed here as a military analyst, so I would refer to a political or a constitutional expert to give a more worthwhile answer to your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. That is all today. We have no further time. We will refer in due course to find an occasion for this. We must adjourn now. Tuesday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, with that conclusion of cross-examination, I can waive re-examination so we can complete with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have to end it now. If this witness is prepared to give it up, so well, but we have no further time today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I understand that but I think the position is Mr. Tapuskovic has finished, I have no re-examination, so he's free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If he's finished, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have not finished. I was reckoning with 20 minutes, as you led me believe, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. In due course. We will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 3rd day of February, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
